card.hook: You know that moment when a canal bends, the brick houses lean in, and a tall tower pops up at the far end like it was placed there on purpose? That's Rozenhoedkaai, and the Belfry is the finishing touch.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rozenhoedkaai, the stone quay on the south side of the canal, near the bend where the Dijver meets the Groenerei. It's a short walk from the Markt. Face along the canal bend so the Belfry rises over the rooftops at the far end.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the canal bend, the guild houses and the reflections all in one shot. Then try 2x to bring the Belfry closer. Skip 0.5x unless you want the whole quay, because it makes the tower look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the canal bend in the lower half so the reflections get lots of room, and keep the tower near a vertical line so it stands up straight.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or blue hour, when the canal reflections look their best. At blue hour, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows into your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: On Rozenhoedkaai, stand on the stone quay by the canal bend with the Belfry behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the tower peek over your shoulder. The Markt is the second option: stand next to the statue in the middle of the square, but go very early or the crowds will photobomb you.
card.ask_someone: On the Markt, stand near the central statue so the tower fills the background, and ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back, facing you and the Belfry.
card.rules_and_safety: Rozenhoedkaai is a free public quay. Climbing the Belfry itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots from three spots a few steps apart along the quay, then pick the one where the Belfry looks tallest and the reflections look best.
card.good_to_know: The Belfry has stood on the Markt since around 1240, when Bruges was a major centre of the Flemish cloth trade. It's 83 metres tall and leans about 87 centimetres to the east. It once reached 102 metres, but the wooden spire burned down in 1741 and was never replaced. The tower has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1999.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rozenhoedkaai, the stone quay on the south side of the canal, near the bend where the Dijver meets the Groenerei. It's a short walk from the Markt. Face along the canal bend so the Belfry rises over the rooftops at the far end.

card.hook: In 1832 someone decided the grand staircase of this little basilica should shuffle 4 metres back and be rebuilt. It's still the showpiece, with stone carving, gold details and the Town Hall all squeezed into one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand out in Burg square, across from the basilica, with the Town Hall right beside it. Face the facade and step back until the whole front fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole facade in. If you can't step back far enough, tap 0.5x, and use 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out the gilded statues on the staircase.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the building with the vertical lines so the facade doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go before 10:00 or after 17:00, when the square is quieter. Fewer people in your shot is always a win.
card.selfie_here: Stand in Burg square directly in front of the ornate facade with the basilica behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the building rise over your shoulder. For a different backdrop, the little Gruuthuse Hof courtyard right next to the basilica gives you another angle.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the opposite corner of Burg square, facing the basilica, while you stand with your back to it so the whole facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the outside are fine from Burg square. Photography is not allowed in the upper chapel where the relic is displayed, and you may be asked to delete any photos taken there. Visiting times for the interior vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the gilded statues on the staircase and see how many rulers you can fit in one shot without clipping anyone's head.
card.good_to_know: The basilica began in 1134 as a private chapel for the Count of Flanders, was finished by 1157, and became a minor basilica in 1923. It's really two chapels stacked together: a dark Romanesque lower chapel and a Gothic Revival upper chapel that holds the famous relic. The staircase outside was built between 1529 and 1533 in late Gothic and Renaissance style.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand out in Burg square, across from the basilica, with the Town Hall right beside it. Face the facade and step back until the whole front fits.

card.hook: Everyone queues along Rozenhoedkaai with their elbows out, all taking the same shot. Slip away to a quiet square on the same canal and you can have guild buildings and glowing streetlights almost to yourself.
card.stand_here: Stand in Jan Van Eyckplein, on the same canal as Rozenhoedkaai, which is about 500 m (roughly 519 m) to the south along the canal. Face along the canal so the guild buildings and the streetlight reflections are in front of you.
card.zoom: Stay at zoom 1x for the canal and its reflections. If you walk down to the quay later, zoom 0.5x fits the whole row of gables, and zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) picks out the Belfry above the roofs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the canal edge up with a horizontal line, so the buildings sit level and the reflections fill the lower half.
card.best_time: Go after dark for Jan Van Eyckplein. One guide says it's largely empty after about 9 PM, and early morning works too if you want the square to yourself. For the quay, sunrise or blue hour is calmest, because it's very busy during the day.
card.selfie_here: Pick Rozenhoedkaai quay itself, with the canal bend and the medieval houses behind you, and use the front camera at 0.5x so lots of the scene fits over your shoulder. For fewer people and more green, walk further along the quay toward the Groenerei junction, where trees hang over the water.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Nepomucenusbrug, the bridge over the Dijver, while you stand on the quay, so they can frame you with the canal bend behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch your footing while you pose near the water, because the stone and brick paving is uneven in places.
card.challenge: Take one low shot on the quay where the gabled houses rise out of the water, then one from the square at night, and see which one you'd frame on your wall.
card.good_to_know: Rozenhoedkaai is a free public space and is open at all times, though it's very busy during the day. Jan Van Eyckplein is described as quieter and far less photographed than the quay. For the classic view of the canal curving towards the quay, with willows and the Belfry spire, try Nepomucenusbrug.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Jan Van Eyckplein, on the same canal as Rozenhoedkaai, which is about 500 m (roughly 519 m) to the south along the canal. Face along the canal so the guild buildings and the streetlight reflections are in front of you.

card.hook: Here's a museum where the best photo might happen before you even buy a ticket. The paintings inside are famous, but the front of the building is your souvenir.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map at the Groeningemuseum, facing the entrance and front of the building. If there's room, step back a few paces so more of the front fits in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the whole building. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the entrance or a sign.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide brighter or darker: darker if the sky is bright and the front looks gloomy, brighter on a dull day if the walls look grey.
card.best_time: Soft morning light or an overcast sky is kind to the building front. Give yourself a couple of minutes outside for a good set of pictures.
card.selfie_here: Try the small garden outside the museum on the Dijver side, reached through the Dijver 12 gate. Two guides call it photogenic, though it won't have the museum building behind you. Use the front camera, and switch to 0.5x if you want more of the garden in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: A third-party pass site says selfie sticks aren't allowed at the museum. Personal photos without flash are generally okay inside, but some special exhibitions may restrict photos. Check the museum's own rules before you go, and also check whether it's open: Visit Bruges says it closes on 11 January 2027 for a four-year refurbishment.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole front, then one close-up of a sign or detail nobody else would notice, and see if you can spot it again later in your camera roll.
card.good_to_know: The Groeningemuseum is Bruges's municipal art museum, with Flemish and Belgian painting spanning six centuries, from Jan van Eyck to Marcel Broodthaers. Van Eyck's Madonna with Canon van der Paele (1436) is one of the headline works. The museum stands on the site of the medieval Eekhout Abbey.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map at the Groeningemuseum, facing the entrance and front of the building. If there's room, step back a few paces so more of the front fits in.

card.hook: Most people cross the Bonifaciusbrug looking straight ahead. Turn round, and there's a 115.6-metre brick tower standing over the canal like it's waiting for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Bonifaciusbrug, on the north-east side of the Church of Our Lady, about 1 minute on foot from it. Turn to face south-west, back towards the tower, so the canal and the Gruuthuse garden run in a line towards it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the canal, garden, ivy and tower in one frame, which helps because the bridge is narrow and you can't step back. Zoom 1x looks calmer and less stretched, and zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) gets you a tighter shot of the brick tower with the water below.
card.make_it_pop: Hold your phone upright, switch on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: The sun clears the church roofline in mid-morning, but that's also when the tour groups arrive. Get there early and take a few frames in a row, because people keep wandering through.
card.selfie_here: Do it on the Bonifaciusbrug. Use the front camera at 0.5x, turn your back to the church and let the tower rise over your shoulder, just as it does when you glance behind you on the way across.
card.ask_someone: On the small square on Mariastraat, where you can see the brick tower, ask someone to stand back far enough to fit the whole tower in, with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is narrow, so keep your phone steady while others pass. Inside the church, photos are fine in the free nave but not in the museum section. Flash is usually banned, and the photography rules posted inside apply, especially near Michelangelo's Madonna.
card.challenge: Keep a bit of the bridge railing or some ivy in the bottom corner and see if you can make the tower look even taller above it.
card.good_to_know: The tower is 115.6 metres high, which makes it the tallest structure in Bruges and the third tallest brickwork church tower in the world. The church dates mainly from the 13th to 15th centuries, and its Gothic flying buttresses were built in the 1270s and 80s. Inside, you'll find a Michelangelo Madonna and Child, plus a chapel made in 1482 for Lodewijk van Gruuthuse as his private place of worship.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Bonifaciusbrug, on the north-east side of the Church of Our Lady, about 1 minute on foot from it. Turn to face south-west, back towards the tower, so the canal and the Gruuthuse garden run in a line towards it.

card.hook: You're mid-stroll down a shopping street, bags in hand, and suddenly a fortress of a tower pops up over the rooftops. That's St. Salvator's, and it's very hard to miss.
card.stand_here: Stand along Steenstraat, the shopping street the cathedral sits just off, and face the cathedral's south-west side where the tower rises. The street's lines point straight at it, so let them do the work.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the tower with the street leading up to it. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the stonework and the top of the tower. Use 0.5x only if the street is too tight to fit the tower in.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines, and hold your phone level so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter on the shopping street, which gives you the clearest view. Mid-morning to afternoon works too, but expect people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to Sint-Salvatorskerkhof, the square outside the cathedral entrance, and turn so the church is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the tower over your shoulder. You can also try Oostmeers, walking north on the cobbles, with the cathedral's spire above the roofs behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand on Steenstraat with the tower in the frame behind you, and ask a passer-by to take your photo from a few steps back along the street.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is a place of worship, so dress modestly. Photography inside is allowed without flash, but check the rules on the day.
card.challenge: Take one shot from Steenstraat and one from the churchyard, then pick a winner. Bonus points if you can spot the difference in how tall the tower feels.
card.good_to_know: The tower is neo-Romanesque and 99 metres high. A fire brought the roof down in 1839, and English architect Robert Chantrell designed the new tower. Its base is the oldest part of the church, from the 12th century. The church became a cathedral in 1834, which is why the tower was made taller and more imposing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand along Steenstraat, the shopping street the cathedral sits just off, and face the cathedral's south-west side where the tower rises. The street's lines point straight at it, so let them do the work.

card.hook: Picture a lake so still it hands you a second set of towers upside down, with a swan or two gliding through the middle like they were hired for the job. That's Minnewater, and it's one of the calmest spots on the map for a phone photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Minnewaterbrug, the pedestrian bridge over the lake. Face the water so the swans, the park and the reflected towers are all in front of you, with the Gunpowder Tower close by.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic view of water, swans and towers. Tap 0.5x to squeeze in more of the lake and park, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a swan or a tower reflection.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the horizon level, and put the water in the lower half so the towers and trees fill the top.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon in spring or autumn gives soft light and usually fewer people. Golden hour, just before sunset, is another good choice.
card.selfie_here: On the Minnewater bridge, use the front camera with the water and park behind you, and try 0.5x to fit more in. Or stand right next to the Sashuis (the lock keeper's house) at the water's edge for a historic building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a bigger backdrop, stand by the water with Minnewater Castle (Kasteel Minnewater) behind you and ask someone to stand on the far bank of the lake facing the castle, so the castle and lake fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The lake, park and bridge are open public space, but check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any buildings nearby.
card.challenge: Get a swan sitting on one of your grid lines with the towers reflected perfectly behind it, and wait for the ripples to settle first.
card.good_to_know: Minnewater is a lake and park in Bruges, with the Gunpowder Tower standing close by. The Sashuis is the lock keeper's house beside the water, and it's a quieter spot if the bridge is busy. It's a place to stroll rather than rush, so walk round the water's edge and try a few angles.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Minnewaterbrug, the pedestrian bridge over the lake. Face the water so the swans, the park and the reflected towers are all in front of you, with the Gunpowder Tower close by.

Sources differ on the exact selfie vantage point (bridge versus lockhouse), so both are given. Some pages are 1 to 6 years old.

card.hook: Picture a rich Bruges family in 1472 who wanted to get to church without going outside, so they built a chapel that links their house to the Church of Our Lady. That link is the detail to hunt for here.
card.stand_here: Start at the Gruuthusemuseum, right beside the Church of Our Lady. The phone icon sits at the centre of the museum, so walk along the street until the whole building fits, then face it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the whole building. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x. Then go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for windows, details and the chapel link towards the church.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roof and window edges with them, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Early morning or a softly overcast day gives gentle light and fewer people in your shot. Check the official site for opening and entry details before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the museum's covered balcony, which looks over the Bonifacius Bridge and the Church of Our Lady. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the bridge and church fill the view behind you. The Bonifacius Bridge itself is another popular spot for a selfie.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Dijver path along the canal, across from the museum's canal-side facade, and ask someone to take your photo so the whole building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside, photos without flash for personal use are generally fine, but check the signs or ask staff. The building has stairs and no elevators, which can be tough for visitors with mobility issues.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the chapel link and the church share the frame, then one tight shot of a window, and see which one you like more.
card.good_to_know: The house gets its name from gruit, which was stored and taxed in a building on this spot, probably from the 13th century. The city bought it in 1875 and it was restored between 1883 and 1895, so the outside is partly original and partly rebuilt. Inside you'll find tapestries, bobbin lace, furniture and a small bronze bell thought to date from about 1245.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the Gruuthusemuseum, right beside the Church of Our Lady. The phone icon sits at the centre of the museum, so walk along the street until the whole building fits, then face it.

card.hook: Look closely at the front of Bruges City Hall and you'll spot a fix from 1766: someone moved the left-hand door so the whole front would look more balanced. Now it's your turn to make the facade look good in a photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Burg Square, at the south-central edge of the square, facing the City Hall facade. The Basilica of the Holy Blood should peek in at the left corner of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole front in one shot. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the turrets, niches and carved details. Use 0.5x only if you're close and the building won't fit.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the edges of the facade up with them so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the hour after sunrise, when the square is usually emptier and the basilica shows at the left corner in early light. The hour before sunset is also worth a try.
card.selfie_here: Try Burg Square beside one of the ornate lamp posts, so the lamp post frames the City Hall details behind you. Use the front camera, switch to the wider front option (0.5x) if your phone has one, and hold the phone a bit higher so the facade shows over your shoulder. The arch on Blinde Ezelstraat, beside the City Hall, is another framing idea, but treat it as a bonus rather than a sure thing.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the south-central edge of Burg Square, pointing the camera at the City Hall facade, while you pose by a lamp post with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash inside the City Hall may be restricted, so check the signs if you go in. The outside views cost nothing, but the interior is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the door that was moved in 1766, then get a photo that makes the front look nicely balanced anyway.
card.good_to_know: The Stadhuis was built between 1376 and 1421 and is one of the oldest city halls in the former Burgundian Netherlands. Its design inspired the city halls of Brussels, Ghent, Leuven and Oudenaarde. The statues on the front were destroyed at the time of the French Revolution and have been renewed since.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Burg Square, at the south-central edge of the square, facing the City Hall facade. The Basilica of the Holy Blood should peek in at the left corner of your frame.

card.hook: Here's a rare thing: a big European square where you can stand in the middle and not dodge a single car. The Markt has been mostly traffic-free since 1995–96, so the Belfry gets the whole stage to itself.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Markt, in the centre of the square, and face the Belfry on the south side. The stepped-gable guild houses frame the tower on either side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the Belfry, the guild houses and the cobbles into one shot. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the top of the tower or the statue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the Belfry on a vertical line, and keep your phone level so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best bet, with the cleanest views and fewer people. After dark the Belfry is lit and the cobbles are quieter, so use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the statue of Jan Breydel and Pieter de Coninck, near the centre of the square, with the Belfry rising behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it so the tower fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The cobbles are uneven, so wear comfy shoes. If you want to go up the Belfry or into any building, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Take the same Belfry shot at 0.5x, 1x and 2x, then pick the winner and tell your friends it was the plan all along.
card.good_to_know: The Markt has been a gathering place since the 10th century, and its first international fair was around 1200. The statue in the middle honours Jan Breydel and Pieter de Coninck, who fought at the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302, and it was unveiled in 1887. The square covers about a hectare.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Markt, in the centre of the square, and face the Belfry on the south side. The stepped-gable guild houses frame the tower on either side.

card.hook: You walk down a narrow, shady alley with your phone half out, and then the whole of Burg opens up in front of you like someone pulled back a curtain. That's the moment to catch.
card.stand_here: Stand in Blinde Ezelstraat, the arched passage on the south side of the City Hall, right where you step out into the square. Face the Gothic City Hall and let the arch wrap around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the arch and the whole City Hall facade fit in one shot. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or higher (depending on your phone) to pick out the Basilica's statues and facade details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the phone level so the building doesn't lean, then tap the facade and slide it a little darker so the bright stonework keeps its detail against the dark arch.
card.best_time: The first hour after sunrise is lovely, and the square is calmer before 10:00 and after 17:00. Midday is usually the busiest, so expect company.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Basilica of the Holy Blood, on the Burg corner, by the lion statues at its door, with the facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit higher so the building fills the background. For a shadier, moodier option, take one under the Blinde Ezelstraat arch, with the City Hall over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the opposite corner of the square from the Basilica, while you stand in front of it with the facade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stick to exterior views of the Basilica, because photography of the relic and the upper chapel inside isn't allowed. If you fancy the little Gruuthuse Hof courtyard beside the Basilica, check on arrival that it's open.
card.challenge: Take the same City Hall shot at 0.5x and 1x, then pick the winner. Which one makes the arch feel more dramatic?
card.good_to_know: Burg is Middle Dutch for "fortress", and the square began as a walled stronghold where the Roman road met the Reie canal. Steen Castle, a residence of the Counts of Flanders, once stood on the western side. The square roughly doubled in size, to around 1.1 hectares, when Saint Donatian's Cathedral was demolished in 1799.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Blinde Ezelstraat, the arched passage on the south side of the City Hall, right where you step out into the square. Face the Gothic City Hall and let the arch wrap around it.

selfie_spots.why: The lion statues that guard the Basilica entrance give a recognisable foreground, and the Basilica facade fills the background of the square's most distinctive corner.

card.hook: Picture a three-arched stone bridge, still water and a row of whitewashed houses so tidy they look freshly ironed. That's the view of the Princely Beguinage Ten Wijngaerde that everyone shares, and it's easy to see why.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Wijngaard Bridge (Wijngaardbrug) and face the white arched gateway at the far end, with the whitewashed houses rising behind it. From the bridge, the middle of the beguinage is to the west, about 2 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic gate-and-houses shot. Inside the courtyard, switch to zoom 0.5x so the lawn and gabled houses fit. Try zoom 2x or more (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the arch of the gateway.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white walls, then slide the brightness to darker just a little so they stay bright but don't wash out, and switch on the gridlines to keep the walls straight.
card.best_time: Go very early in the morning if you can. You'll beat the tour groups and have the bridge nearly to yourself.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Wijngaard Bridge in front of the main gate, with the whitewashed entrance behind you. Use the front camera, and if yours has a wide option, use it to fit more of the gate over your shoulder. Inside, stay on the paved paths of the central courtyard, not the lawns, with the white houses behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the Wijngaardplein, the square in front of the beguinage, and ask them to face it so the whole front of the complex fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working convent, so keep your voice down, stay off the grass where signs ask, and don't point your phone into residents' windows or doorways. One guide says drones aren't permitted, and another says commercial photography needs permission. Watch for horse carriages and take care on the cobblestones.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice: once on the bridge, then again from inside the courtyard. Which one would you send to your friends?
card.good_to_know: This is the only preserved beguinage in Bruges. It was founded around 1244 and is now a Benedictine convent, so no beguines live there any more. Inside are about thirty white-painted houses from the late 16th to 18th centuries, with a Gothic church among them. The arched gateway at the far end of the bridge dates from 1776.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Wijngaard Bridge (Wijngaardbrug) and face the white arched gateway at the far end, with the whitewashed houses rising behind it. From the bridge, the middle of the beguinage is to the west, about 2 minutes on foot.

card.hook: Look for a golden half-moon on warm brown brick, and you've found it. The Halve Maan Brewery is one of the easiest buildings in Bruges to pick out, even if you only have a minute.
card.stand_here: Head to Walplein in the centre of Bruges and step back into the open part of the square. Face the brewery front, with the restaurants behind you. The phone icon on the map marks the brewery itself, so give yourself some room.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade in. Then try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the logo and the little arched doorway. If you can't step back far enough, zoom 0.5x will squeeze it all in, so keep the building centred to stop the edges leaning.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brick wall, then slide the picture a touch darker if the gold logo looks washed out.
card.best_time: Daylight is best for the warm brick and the gold logo. Earlier in the day is likely to be calmer, with fewer groups at the entrance.
card.selfie_here: Walplein is a famously photogenic square, so this is your selfie spot. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and turn so the brewery is over your shoulder. Check the screen to see how much of the building made it in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out on the open square facing the brewery front, while you stand in front of the building so the arched entrance and golden half-moon logo are in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go on a brewery tour, expect lots of stairs. Wear comfortable shoes and be ready for the climb.
card.challenge: Get the golden logo and the arched doorway in one frame with no tour group in it. You may have to wait for a gap, so be patient.
card.good_to_know: The brewery's address is Walplein 26. The views from the roof and tower are part of the paid tour, and they show the city rather than the brewery. If you want to go inside, check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Walplein in the centre of Bruges and step back into the open part of the square. Face the brewery front, with the restaurants behind you. The phone icon on the map marks the brewery itself, so give yourself some room.

card.hook: A windmill with its sails out, standing on a grassy bank with nothing but sky behind it, is about as easy a photo as Bruges gets. Walk down the slope and it's all in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in Kruisvest, on the grassy slope below the rampart, and turn to face the mill. From here you'll be looking south-west, with the sails and the body of the mill sitting together against the sky.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the whole mill from the slope. If you wander closer along the path and the sails get cut off, tap 0.5x. For a tighter shot of just the sails, try 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the mill on one of the vertical lines, and leave a little sky above the sails so they don't get clipped.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is the classic time, but from the slope the low sun will be in front of you. If that happens, tap the mill and slide it darker so the sky stays blue and the sails keep their detail. For the sun behind you, come in the morning.
card.selfie_here: Head up onto the grassy mound next to the mill, on the Kruisvest ramparts. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more in, and hold the phone a little low so the mill sits over your shoulder. Take a quick test shot to check the angle.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone on the canal path at the foot of the grassy mound to shoot up at you from lower down, so the whole mill fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: If you climb up the mill, go carefully, because there are no safety rails.
card.challenge: Get the sails against the sky with the tower perfectly straight, then take a second one with you pulling a silly windmill pose.
card.good_to_know: Sint-Janshuismolen stands on the rampart edge of Bruges, next to Kruisvest park and close to the St Anne's Quarter. Going inside can be seasonal and the mill may be closed in winter, so check before you go. Photos from outside still work really well.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Kruisvest, on the grassy slope below the rampart, and turn to face the mill. From here you'll be looking south-west, with the sails and the body of the mill sitting together against the sky.

card.hook: Picture a narrow little bridge, old brick houses on both sides, and a canal that runs straight to the Church of Our Lady tower. That's the classic Bruges shot, and you get it without any fuss.
card.stand_here: Stand on Bonifaciusbrug itself, right where the phone icon is, and face north. The canal runs away between the brick facades with the tower rising behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the canal, the facades and the tower all in. Tap 2x if you want the tower a bit closer, or 0.5x if you'd like more of the bridge and the buildings beside you.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the canal in the middle so it leads the eye straight to the tower, with a little water in the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Go early, before the tour groups arrive around mid-morning. One guide also suggests late evening.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement at the bridge's end, next to the portico entrance of the Nuit Blanche guest house and art gallery. One guide calls it a lovely photo spot. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold your phone so the bridge sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the canal-side path on the south bank, a few metres past the bridge, stepping down slightly toward the water and facing north, while you pose on the bridge with the tower rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge has steps at both ends and isn't wheelchair accessible. The stone deck gets noticeably slippery in wet weather and the canal walls are low, so watch your footing and keep a firm grip on your phone. It's a small bridge, so take your photo, then step aside for the next person.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the gridlines on and the canal dead centre, then spot whether the tower lines up with the middle of the picture.
card.good_to_know: Bonifaciusbrug is a small, narrow pedestrian bridge over one of Bruges' canals. Photo guides call the view from it the classic angle. For a picture of the bridge itself, Arentshof gives you the view from the water's edge, with the Church of Our Lady tower behind. It's the angle most often cited as the best photo of the bridge.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Bonifaciusbrug itself, right where the phone icon is, and face north. The canal runs away between the brick facades with the tower rising behind.

selfie_spots.detail: on the little stairs that lead down from the path to the canal edge next to the Gruuthuse Palace
selfie_spots.why: It offers a lower, less obvious vantage point on the bridge, which a blogger calls a unique photo location.

selfie_spots.detail: on the pavement at the bridge's end, beside the portico entrance of the Nuit Blanche guest house and art gallery
selfie_spots.why: The portico entrance gives a framed setting next to the bridge, which one guide calls a lovely photo.

ask_someone_spot.detail: step down slightly toward the water, then face back north toward the bridge with the Church of Our Lady tower rising behind it

sources.title: Boniface Bridge (Bonifaciusbrug) - Bruges - Nomado Travel

selfie_research.safety: In wet weather the stone deck of the bridge becomes noticeably slippery, and the canal walls on both sides are low, so watch your footing, especially when carrying camera gear.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found states rules about selfie sticks or tripods, so the rules list is empty. The two selfie spots come from a single blog, which describes them as photo spots rather than as selfie positions, so whether the landmark sits directly behind a selfie-taker there is inferred, not confirmed. Sources differ on the address: one gives Groeninge 6 behind the Church of Our Lady, another places it between Gruuthuse and Arentshof, and another mentions Arents Courtyard. The coordinates on Top.Vlaanderen (51.20504, 3.22541) are very close to your position. The ask-someone spot is taken from the Nomado page, which describes the south-bank view as the best photograph of the bridge rather than a passer-by instruction, so I adapted it.

card.hook: Spin slowly on the spot and you'll see roofs, doorways and old brick walls from different centuries, all packed close together. You hardly need to walk anywhere to get a good photo here.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon, right in the middle of the Old St. John's Hospital grounds beside the Church of Our Lady. Then turn around and pick whichever wall, gable or doorway looks best.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for most views, and use 0.5x if you can only step back a little. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out gables and windows, and skip 0.5x for close-up details because it stretches the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the vertical walls with the vertical lines so the buildings don't look like they're leaning.
card.best_time: Go early in the day or later in the afternoon, when there are usually fewer people and the light is softer. A cloudy day is fine too, because the brickwork looks nicely even.
card.selfie_here: Try the Mariastraat Bridge (Mariabrug). Stand on the bridge facing the canal houses, so the hospital is behind you, then use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more in. Have a quick look on the spot to check the hospital really is in your frame.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on Mariabrug and ask them to frame you with the hospital across the water.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the grounds and the Hans Memling museum may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find an archway or doorway and use it as a frame for one shot, then see if you can take a second one with no people in it.
card.good_to_know: The hospital was founded in the mid-12th century to care for sick pilgrims and travellers, and it holds some of the oldest surviving hospital buildings in Europe. It was nearly demolished in the 1860s but was saved by Gothic Revival supporters, especially Englishmen living in Bruges. It stopped working as a hospital in 1977, and part of it is now the Hans Memling museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon, right in the middle of the Old St. John's Hospital grounds beside the Church of Our Lady. Then turn around and pick whichever wall, gable or doorway looks best.

selfie_spots.name: Mariastraat Bridge (Mariabrug), Bruges
selfie_spots.detail: on the bridge, facing the side with the canal houses so the hospital is behind you
selfie_spots.why: One travel guide says the bridge has photogenic views from both sides, with a canal house on one side and the hospital on the other, so facing the houses puts the hospital at your back.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was found; the others were not confirmed for a selfie with the hospital behind. The Mariastraat Bridge placement is an inference from a page saying one side shows the canal houses and the other shows the hospital, so check the bridge on the ground before relying on it. Both spots are on the same bridge. No page mentioned selfie stick or tripod rules. Photography inside the museum is described as permitted without flash (brugge.info), which is not a selfie-stick rule, so I left it out of rules. The bridge is said to get crowded, so an early visit is suggested (wanderlusterprincess). Nothing in the sources gave a safety point.

card.hook: Jan van Eyckplein is a pretty little square, but the picture everyone wants is taken from a short walk away, on a bridge. Go there and the tower and its twin in the canal line up like they planned it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Koningsbrug, the bridge over the Spiegelrei. The square is about 170 m to the south-west, so turn round and look back towards it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the tower, the square and the reflection into one frame. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for just the tower and water, and 0.5x if you turn to look south at the guild-house fronts.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the water line on the lower third, so the reflection fills the bottom of the picture and the tower rises above it.
card.best_time: Early morning or a soft, overcast day is best, because the water is calm and the reflection is cleanest. Blue hour after sunset looks lovely too, so switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the bridge wall to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera and try 0.5x to squeeze more in. Stand with your back to the scene so the buildings sit over your shoulder, and hold the phone level so they don't lean.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Koningsbrug and shoot back towards the square while you stand in the square facing the bridge (it's our best guess at the setup, so check it works on site).
card.challenge: Catch the reflection with no boat or passer-by crossing it, and see how many tries it takes you.
card.good_to_know: The square is named after the Northern Renaissance painter Jan van Eyck. It sits where Academiestraat, the Spiegelrei and Spanjaardstraat meet, beside a canal. The Gothic tower you're photographing belongs to the Poortersloge, and no ticket is needed for this viewpoint.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Koningsbrug, the bridge over the Spiegelrei. The square is about 170 m to the south-west, so turn round and look back towards it.

ask_someone_spot.name: Koningsbrug (Koningstraat bridge) over the canal next to Jan Van Eyckplein
ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand on the bridge facing Jan Van Eyck Square. Kirstie Will Travel describes this as the spot for the best canal view of the square. Dailytravelpill names the same bridge as the best view toward the square. The square should then be in the frame behind the visitor, who stands in the square facing the bridge. The pages do not describe this arrangement, so confirm it on site.

sources.title: The 15 best Instagram spots in Bruges - Kirstie Will Travel
16 Bruges photography locations - BEST viewpoints - Daily Travel Pill

selfie_research.notes: No page I found describes a selfie with Jan van Eyckplein behind the person, so I returned no selfie spot rather than guess. The Koningsbrug bridge is the best-documented viewpoint, but the sources describe shooting toward the square, not with it behind the subject. The ask-someone position is my inference from those sources, and the visitor's placement in the square is not stated by any page. Chasing Hippoz also suggests the stone bridge at the north end of the square, looking south toward the guild facades, as a photo position; I did not use it because it is not named as a bridge in the sources. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules for this square. Chasing Hippoz mentions a tripod only as a night-photography tip, not as a rule. No page mentions a safety point.

card.hook: This church isn't trying to impress you with gold or spires. It's plain brick and one stocky tower, and that's exactly why it looks so good on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Sint-Jakobsplein, the square the church sits on. From there the church lies to the north-east, so face that way and you'll see the brick walls and the heavy tower rising above the roofline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the walls and tower in together. If the church won't fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the top of the tower and the brickwork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the tall walls stay straight instead of leaning inwards.
card.best_time: Soft daylight, like morning or late afternoon, suits brick best because the warm colour really shows. In harsh midday sun the shadows on the walls can get strong.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and tap 0.5x if your phone offers it, so more of the church fits in. Turn so the tower sits over your shoulder and hold the phone a little higher than your face.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go inside, don't use flash. Opening details may have changed, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Walk around the building and find the squat tower peeking over the roofline from three different side streets, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: The church dates from around 1240. It was enlarged considerably in 1459, when Bruges was growing rich, and the Duke of Burgundy was among its patrons. The inside was remodelled in Baroque style in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. You might see it called St. Jacob's, but that's a mix-up, because Flemish uses one word for both James and Jacob.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Sint-Jakobsplein, the square the church sits on. From there the church lies to the north-east, so face that way and you'll see the brick walls and the heavy tower rising above the roofline.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific selfie spot with St. James's Church behind the visitor, or a specific spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole church, so I have left both empty rather than guess. The closest leads were a Flickr photo page describing the church as sitting on the corner of Sint-Jakobsstraat 'just before the curb' (a description of the building's location, not a recommended vantage point), and Wikimedia Commons categories for Sint-Jakobsplein and Sint-Jakobsstraat, which list photos but name no vantage point. Address details conflict across sources: Sint-Jakobsplein 1 (Flickr, Petit Futé, Wikidata), Sint-Jakobsstraat 5 (brugge.info), Sint-Jakobsstraat 45 (London Concert Choir), Moerstraat 1 (Mapcarta), and Sint-Annaplein (Tripadvisor). The coordinates you gave (51.21057, 3.22063) match the church's Wikidata position (about 51°12'38"N, 3°13'14"E), so the location is consistent. The only photography rule found is that photography inside is allowed without flash (brugge.info), which concerns the interior and not the exterior selfie or photo spots, so I have not listed it under rules.
